question: Printed circuit boards (PCBs) and electronics manufacturing services (EMS) are indispensable components of Europe’s technology ecosystem. Their relevance continues to grow as digital systems become more complex, and as the reliability and quality of these downstream manufacturing steps increasingly determine the safety, performance and resilience of final products.

Europe’s position in both segments has eroded dramatically: China now accounts for 58.7 % of global PCB manufacturing, while the EU’s share has fallen from 20 % in 2000 to just 2 %. In EMS, Europe’s share has declined from 22 % to 10 %.
This growing dependency raises significant concerns for the EU’s technological sovereignty and industrial competitiveness, and the security of its critical infrastructure and defence systems. 1.

Does the Commission intend to provide targeted support for European PCB and EMS manufacturing through EU instruments, and how might the forthcoming revision of the Chips Act1 strengthen their role within Europe’s microelectronics ecosystem?

How does the Commission assess the impact of the current customs regime, under which base materials are subject to duties while finished PCBs enter duty-free, on Europe’s competitiveness and security of supply, and whether existing trade defence instruments are adequate to address market distortions in this sector?
Is the Commission planning to introduce European-sourcing criteria for PCBs and EMS for use in critical infrastructure and defence-related applications to reduce strategic vulnerabilities?
OJ L 229, 18.9.2023, p. 1, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1781/oj.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.3.2026) The revision of the Chips Act1 is ongoing, with the proposal for a Chips Act 2 foreseen in spring 2026. Preparatory work is carried out in an inclusive way, with the possibility for stakeholders to voice their priorities via the call for evidence.

Printed circuit boards and electronics manufacturing services are not excluded from the scope of the Chips Act but the Commission is assessing whether the first-of-a-kind definition needs to be clarified to provide legal certainty to actors in the semiconductor value chain planning investments in the EU. The level of customs duty rate applicable depends on the tariff classification of the goods.

Levels of bound duty rates, including where it is ‘duty-free’, result from EU commitments under the 1994 General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade. The Commission is committed to protecting EU industries from unfair competition where it finds that EU industry is suffering from dumped and/or subsidised imports. Industries can contact the Commission’s trade defence services2 for such issues.

The Commission aims to tackle strategic dependencies as cybersecurity risks. The proposed Cybersecurity Act 23 aims to reduce risks in the EU’s information and communication technology (ICT) supply chain from third-country suppliers with cybersecurity concerns. It sets a trusted ICT supply chain security framework using a harmonised, proportionate and risk-based approach.
